kicker: tools · hybrid encryption in one file
tagline: RSA-4096 and AES-256-GCM in a single HTML file. No server, no dependency, no network call: the browser's own crypto engine and nothing else. Read the whole thing before you trust it.
launchSub: Generate · encrypt · decrypt · keys never leave the tab
titleTail: RSA-4096 and AES-256 in one HTML file
lede: A 4096-bit RSA-OAEP key can encrypt about 446 bytes. That's a sentence, not a document. So RSA never touches the message at all: it encrypts a key, and that key encrypts the message. CryptoVault does all of it for real, in your browser, with crypto.subtle; the ciphertext it prints is the actual output, not a stand-in.

features.d: a new random key for every message, used once, so a compromised message compromises nothing else.
fast, any size, and authenticated: tampering is caught on decrypt instead of quietly producing garbage.
256 bytes of key material, comfortably inside RSA's limit. It's the only thing the asymmetric layer ever sees.
the wrapped key, the IV and the ciphertext travel together; only the private key's holder can open it.

cards.n: one file, zero trust in me
cards.html: No dependencies: no npm tree, no CDN, no crypto library to audit. No network: open devtools and watch the network tab stay empty. No storage: keys live in memory for the tab's lifetime. Readable: one file you can scroll to the bottom of. That's the whole security argument, and it only works while it stays small.

scope: It doesn't distribute keys (the actual hard problem), doesn't prove who sent a message (that needs signatures), and served over a network it's only as trustworthy as whoever serves it. For anything that genuinely matters, use age or GPG. This is a working demonstration of the primitives, not audited infrastructure.
closing: A crypto tool that overstates itself is worse than no tool.
